paper.title: 8th IOAA · Final data analysis paper
paper.caveat: The final paper is preserved in six photographed sheets. Its three whole problems differ from the preliminary solution booklet: Black Hole is renumbered, Thermodynamic test is separate, and the observer problem replaces seven Big Dipper stars with four Mizar-system stars and adds uncertainty estimates. Applicable key material is distinguished from variant comparisons; absent final-key portions and the missing orbit-plot annex are explicit.

problems.title: Black Hole in Milky Way
problems.statement:
By observational facts, the scientists admit presence of a black-hole at the center of Milky Way.
At the center of Milky Way, a hypothetical black-hole (Sagittarius A*) is located. A star S* is orbiting the black-hole SA*.

In the table 1 the following data is presented: the date and the angular position coordinates $(\alpha;\beta)$ of the star S* at different moments of the observation. The coordinates represent the angular distances of the projection of the star S* in the coordinates system (U, W), centered on the SA* (see figure 1).
An angular distance of $\varphi=1\,\text{arcsec}$ corresponds to linear distance in the plane of the sky $d=41$ light days, therefore to a scale

$$S_0=\frac d\varphi=41\,\frac{\text{light day}}{\text{arcsec}}.$$

sections.title: c)
General examination instructions
sections.statement:
1) In your folder you will find out the following:
   a) Answer sheets
   b) Draft sheets
   c) The envelope with the subjects in English and the translated version of them in your mother tongue;
2) The solutions of the problems will be written down only on the answer sheets you receive on your desk. **PLEASE WRITE ONLY ON THE PRINTED SIDE OF THE PAPER SHEET. DON'T USE THE REVERSE SIDE.** The evaluator will not take into account what is written on the reverse of the answer sheet.
3) The draft sheets is for your own use to try calculation, write some numbers etc. BEWARE: These papers are not taken into account in evaluation, at the end of the test they will be collected separately. Everything you consider as part of the solutions have to be written on the answer sheets.
4) Each problem have to be started on a new distinct answer sheet.
5) On each answer sheet please fill in the designated boxes as follows:
   a) In PROBLEM NO. box write down only the number of the problem: i.e. 1–3. Each sheet containing the solutions of a certain problem, should have in the box the number of the problem;
   b) In Student ID – fill in your ID you will find on your envelope, consisted of 3 letters and 2 digits.
   c) In page no. box you will fill in the number of page, starting from 1. We advise you to fill this boxes after you finish the test
6) We don't understand your language, but the mathematical language is universal, so use as more relations as you think that your solution will be better understand by the evaluator. If you want to explain in words we kindly ask you to use short English propositions.
7) Use the pen you find out on the desk. It is advisable to use a pencil for the sketches.
8) At the end of the test:
   a) Don't forget to put in order your papers;
   b) Put the answer sheets in the folder 1. Please verify that all the pages contain your ID, correct numbering of the problems and all pages are in the right order and numbered. This is an advantage of a correct understanding your solutions.
   c) Verify with the assistant the correct number of answer sheets used fill in this number on the cover of the folder and sign.
   d) Put the draft papers in the designated folder. Put the test papers back in the envelope.
   e) Go to swim

GOOD LUCK!

solution.statement: The archived booklet labels this problem 2; it is problem 1 on the final photographed paper. Its marking scheme is a) 15 points, b) 10 points and c) 25 points, with 5 points for each of I–V. The calculations below retain the printed numbers and discrepancies.

sections.title: Detailed solution
sections.statement:
Usually the plane of apparent orbit (sky plane) is different from the plane of the relative orbit due to the angle between the two planes ($i=0$).

[[figure p1-sol-fig1]]

In the case of the problem the sky plane and the plane of the relative orbit are the same ($i=0$). See the figure.

[[figure p1-sol-fig2]]

The linear position coordinates $(u,w)$ of the projection of the star S* in the sky plane with the coordinate axes (U, W), having the origin in Sagittarius A*, expressed in light-days are given in table 1. For an angular distance $\varphi=1\,\text{arcsec}$ correspond in sky plane the linear distance $d=41$ light day.

[[figure p1-sol-fig3]]

**Source note:** the first sentence prints $i=0$ while describing different planes; the later sentence also prints $i=0$ for coincident planes. Both are retained.

sections.title: Numeric processing — a)
sections.statement:
From the measurements done on paper system (X, Y):

$$a_{\rm measured}\approx135\,\mathrm{mm};\quad b_{\rm measured}\approx66\,\mathrm{mm};\quad d_{\min}=17\,\mathrm{mm}.$$

Corresponding to the numeric scale:

$$a_{\rm measured}=\varphi_aS;\qquad b_{\rm measured}=\varphi_bS;\qquad d_{\min}^{\rm mes}=\varphi_{\min}S;$$
$$\varphi_a=0.1125\,\text{arcsec};\quad\varphi_b=0.055\,\text{arcsec};\quad\varphi_{d\min}=0{,}01416\,\text{arcsec}.$$

The scale is $1\,\text{arcsec}\longleftrightarrow41$ light day. The source then lists $\varphi_a=0.1125\,\text{arcsec}\longleftrightarrow a$, $\varphi_b=0.055\,\text{arcsec}\longleftrightarrow b$, and $\varphi_{d\min}=0{,}01466\,\text{arcsec}\longleftrightarrow r_{\min}$.

$$a=\frac{0.1125\,\text{arcsec}\cdot41\,\text{light days}}{1\,\text{arcsec}}=4.6125\,\text{light days};$$
$$b=\frac{0.055\,\text{arcsec}\cdot41\,\text{light days}}{1\,\text{arcsec}}=2.255\,\text{light days};$$
$$r_{\min}=\frac{0{,}0146\,\text{arcsec}\cdot41\,\text{light days}}{1\,\text{arcsec}}=0{,}5986\,\text{light days};$$
$$c=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}\approx4{,}0236\,\text{light days};$$
$$r_{\min}=a-c=0{,}5889\,\text{light days};\quad r_{\max}=a+c=8{,}6361\,\text{light days};$$
$$e=\sqrt{1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}}\approx0.87.$$

**Source note:** the three different printed minimum-angle values (0.01416, 0.01466 and 0.0146) and two minimum-distance results are preserved.

sections.title: Numeric processing — c)
sections.statement:
By using the III rd Kepler's law:

$$T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{K(M_{\rm SA*}+M_{\rm S*})}a^3;\qquad M_{\rm SA*}+M_{\rm S*}=\frac{4\pi^2a^3}{KT^2};$$
$$a=4.6125\,\text{light days};\quad T\approx15\,\text{years};\quad K=6{,}67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}};$$
$$1\,\mathrm{ld}\approx2{,}6\cdot10^{13}\,\mathrm m;\quad1\,\text{years}\approx3{,}1\cdot10^7\,\mathrm s;\quad4\pi^2\approx40;$$
$$ (2{,}6)^3\approx17{,}6;\qquad(4.6125)^3\approx10^2;$$
$$M_{\rm SA*}+M_{\rm S*}=\frac{40\cdot10^2\cdot17{,}6\cdot10^{39}}{6{,}67\cdot10^{-11}\cdot225\cdot10^{15}}\,\mathrm{kg}\approx4{,}6\cdot10^{36}\,\mathrm{kg};$$
$$M_{\text{Sun}}\approx1{,}8\cdot10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg};\qquad M_{\rm SA*}+M_{\rm S*}\approx2{,}5\cdot10^6M_{\text{Sun}};$$
$$M_{\rm S*}\ll M_{\rm SA*};\qquad M_{\rm SA*}\approx2{,}5\cdot10^6M_{\text{Sun}}.$$

The printed approximations, gravitational-constant symbol K and solar mass are retained.

problems.title: Thermodynamic test
problems.statement:
An hypothetical shuttle is launched to investigate the atmosphere (100% CO$_2$) of two extrasolar planets P$_1$ and P$_2$. The atmosphere is in static thermodynamic equilibrium. When the shuttle is near each planet, a radio probe is launched toward respective planet, in vertical direction (in the direction of the planet's radius). When the radio probe reaches constant velocity, it starts sending values of the pressure of the atmosphere. In Fig. 3.1 is plotted the atmospheric pressure values (in arbitrary units) as function of the time of descent for the planet P$_1$. When the probe touches the surface of planet P$_1$ it sends the value of the temperature $T_0=700\,\mathrm K$ and the value of the gravitational acceleration $g_0=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

[[figure p2-fig1]]

*The gravitational acceleration on each planet is assumed to be constant during uniform descent of the radio probes.*

figures.caption: Fig. 3.1. Pressure during descent on P₁.
figures.alt: Fig. 3.1. Pressure during descent on P₁.

sections.title: a)
sections.statement: Find the altitude $h_0$ from where the radio probe R$_1$ starts the uniform descent and thus starts the transmitting information.

sections.title: b)
sections.statement: Find the temperature of planet P$_1$ at the altitude $h=39.6\,\mathrm{km}$. You know: The universal gas constant $R=8.3\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$; the molar mass of CO$_2$, $\mu=44\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

sections.title: c)
sections.statement:
In Fig. 3.2 was plotted the atmospheric pressure values (in arbitrary units) as function of the time of descent of the planet P$_2$ atmosphere. When the probe touched the surface of the planet P$_2$, it sends the value of the temperature $T_0=750\,\mathrm K$ and respectively the value of the gravitational acceleration $g_0=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Draw the following dependency graphs for $p=f(h)$ and $T=f(h)$ in the CO$_2$ atmosphere of the planet P$_2$.

figures.caption: Fig. 3.2. Pressure during descent on P₂.
figures.alt: Fig. 3.2. Pressure during descent on P₂.

solution.statement: The matching official key is labelled preliminary Problem 3A. Marking scheme: a) 5 points, b) 10 points, c) 10 points. Printed approximations and the inconsistent temperature in the final table are retained.

sections.title: a) Starting altitude
sections.statement:
As the probe descends, pressure and density increase. At the surface the pressure is $p_{\max}$. Consider a thin atmospheric layer of thickness $\Delta h$ and density $\rho_{\max}$, with gravitational acceleration $g_0$.

[[figure p2-sol-fig1]]

$$p_{\max}=p+\Delta p;\qquad\Delta p=\rho_{\max}g_0\Delta h;\qquad\Delta h=\frac{\Delta p}{\rho_{\max}g_0}.$$

The ideal-gas law gives

$$p_{\max}V=\nu RT_0=\frac m\mu RT_0;\qquad p_{\max}\mu=\frac mVRT_0=\rho_{\max}RT_0;$$
$$\rho_{\max}=\frac{p_{\max}\mu}{RT_0}.$$

For uniform descent, $\Delta h=v\Delta t$, hence

$$v=\frac{\Delta p}{\rho_{\max}g_0\Delta t}=\frac{RT_0\Delta p}{g_0\mu p_{\max}\Delta t}.\tag{1}$$

At the surface point $F(\tau,p_{\max})$, the slope is $\tan\alpha=\Delta p/\Delta t$.

[[figure p2-sol-fig2]]

$$\frac{\Delta p}{p_{\max}\Delta t}=\frac{15}{55\cdot250}=\frac{45}{55\cdot750}=\frac3{2750}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}};$$
$$v=\frac3{2750\,\mathrm s}\frac{8.3\cdot700}{10\cdot44\cdot10^{-3}}=14.4\,\mathrm{m/s};$$
$$h_0=v\tau=14.4\cdot3750\,\mathrm m=54000\,\mathrm m=54\,\mathrm{km}.$$

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Thin atmospheric layer and pressure difference.
figures.alt: Fig. 1. Thin atmospheric layer and pressure difference.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Tangent at the final pressure on P₁.
figures.alt: Fig. 2. Tangent at the final pressure on P₁.

sections.title: b) Temperature at 39.6 km
sections.statement:
The probe reaches $h=39.6\,\mathrm{km}$ at

$$t=\frac{h_0-h}{v}=\frac{54000-39600}{14.4}\,\mathrm s=1000\,\mathrm s.$$

At point C, $p_h=4$ arbitrary units, and $\tan\beta=(\Delta p/\Delta t)_C$.

[[figure p2-sol-fig3-r4]]

$$\left(\frac{\Delta p}{p\Delta t}\right)_C=\frac1{p_h}\left(\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\right)_C=\frac14\frac3{500}=\frac3{2000}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}};$$
$$\left(\frac{p\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_C=p_h\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_C=4\frac{500}3=\frac{2000}3\,\mathrm s.$$

Using (1),

$$v=\left(\frac{\Delta p}{p\Delta t}\right)_C\frac{RT_h}{g_0\mu}=\frac1{p_h}\left(\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\right)_C\frac{RT_h}{g_0\mu};$$
$$T_h=\frac{vg_0\mu}{\frac1{p_h}\left(\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\right)_CR}=p_h\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_C\frac{vg_0\mu}{R};$$
$$T_h=\frac{2000}3\,\mathrm s\cdot\frac{14.4\cdot10\cdot44\cdot10^{-3}}{8.3}=508.9\,\mathrm K.$$

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Tangent at C and surface point F.
figures.alt: Fig. 3. Tangent at C and surface point F.

sections.title: c) Pressure and temperature on P₂
sections.statement:
Use the points F, D, C, B and A of the pressure–time graph.

[[figure p2-sol-fig4]]

$$v=\frac{\Delta p}{p_{\max}\Delta t}\frac{RT_0}{g_0\mu}=\frac{10}{50\cdot500}\frac{8.3\cdot750}{8\cdot44\cdot10^{-3}}\approx7\,\mathrm{m/s};$$
$$h_0=v\tau=7\cdot2000\,\mathrm m=14000\,\mathrm m=14\,\mathrm{km}.$$

At F, $p=50$, $h_F=0$ and $T_F=750\,\mathrm K$.

$$T_D=p_D\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_D\frac{vg_0\mu}{R}=593.7\,\mathrm K;$$
$$h_D=h_0-vt_D=14\,\mathrm{km}-7\cdot1500\,\mathrm m=3.5\,\mathrm{km}.$$

Thus D has $p_D=40$, $h_D=3.5\,\mathrm{km}$, $T_D=593.7\,\mathrm K$.

$$T_C=p_C\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_C\frac{vg_0\mu}{R}=445.3\,\mathrm K;$$
$$h_C=14\,\mathrm{km}-7\cdot1000\,\mathrm m=7\,\mathrm{km}.$$

Thus C has $p_C=30$, $h_C=7\,\mathrm{km}$, $T_C=445.3\,\mathrm K$.

$$T_B=p_B\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_B\frac{vg_0\mu}{R}=296.8\,\mathrm K;$$
$$h_B=14\,\mathrm{km}-7\cdot500\,\mathrm m=10.5\,\mathrm{km}.$$

Thus B has $p_B=20$, $h_B=10.5\,\mathrm{km}$, $T_B=296.8\,\mathrm K$.

$$T_A=p_A\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta p}\right)_A\frac{vg_0\mu}{R}=148.4\,\mathrm K;\qquad h_A=14\,\mathrm{km}.$$

Thus A has $p_A=10$, $h_A=14\,\mathrm{km}$, $T_A=148.4\,\mathrm K$.

| Point | t (s) | p (arbitrary units) | h (km) | T (K) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 10 | 14 | 148.4 |
| B | 500 | 20 | 10.5 | 296.8 |
| C | 1000 | 30 | 7 | 445.3 |
| D | 1500 | 40 | 3.5 | 593.3 |
| F | 2000 | 50 | 0 | 750 |

**Source note:** the intermediate calculation prints 593.7 K for D; the final table prints 593.3 K. Both source values are retained.

problems.title: IOAA Observer on an extrasolar planet
problems.statement:
The Sirius star, located in the constellation of Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky of the Earth. What the observer's eye sees as a single star is actually a binary star system.
The high brightness of Sirius is a consequence of two facts: its intrinsic luminosity and its proximity to the Earth.
The Mizar multiple star system, in the constellation of Ursa Major, consists of 4 stars seen along the same line of sight from the Earth. Some of these stars form a gravitationally bound system.
Let's assume that an observer (observer A) is located on one of the planets of the Sirius system.

Determine:

sections.title: a)
sections.statement: The magnitude of the Sun as seen by observer A ($m_{\text{Sun,Planet}}$).

sections.title: b)
sections.statement: The magnitude of Sirius star system as seen by the observer A ($m_{\text{SY,Planet}}$).

sections.title: c)
sections.statement: The combined intrinsic luminosity of the Mizar system, $L_{\text{Mizar}}$.

sections.title: d)
sections.statement: The average distance between gravitationally bound stars of the Mizar system and Earth.

sections.title: e)
sections.statement: The geocentric angular distance between Mizar system and Sirius, $\Delta\theta$.

sections.title: f)
sections.statement: The physical distance between the gravitationally bound stars of the Mizar system and the observer A ($d_{\text{Mizar,Planet}}$).

sections.title: g)
sections.statement:
The magnitude of the entire Mizar system as seen by the observer A ($m_{\text{Mizar,Planet}}$).

Also estimate amount of errors in all your answers.

sections.title: Data
sections.statement:
The following data may be used:

- $d_{\text{Sirius,Earth}}=2.6\,\mathrm{pc}$ – the Sirius–Earth distance;
- $m_{\text{Sirius,Earth}}=-1.46^{\mathrm m}$ – the apparent magnitude of Sirius measured from the Earth;
- $d_{\text{Sun,Earth}}=1\,\mathrm{AU}$ – the Sun–Earth distance;
- $m_{\text{Sun,Earth}}=-26.78^{\mathrm m}$ – the apparent magnitude of the Sun as seen from Earth;
- $d_{\text{Sirius,Planet}}=10\,\mathrm{AU}$ – distance between Sirius and its planet where the observer A is located.

In the table below information for the stars from the Mizar system as measured from the Earth is given.

| Star number | Name of the star | Apparent magnitude | Parallax (mili arc seconds) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alcor | $3.99\pm0.01$ | $39.91\pm0.13$ |
| 2 | Mizar A | $2.23\pm0.01$ | $38.01\pm1.71$ |
| 3 | Mizar B | $3.86\pm0.01$ | $38.01\pm1.71$ |
| 4 | Sidus Ludoviciana | $7.56\pm0.01$ | $8\pm4$ |

The equatorial coordinates of Mizar system ($\sigma_1$) and respectively of Sirius ($\sigma_2$), located on the heliocentric map are:

$$\alpha_{\text{Mizar}}=\alpha_1=13^{\mathrm h}23^{\mathrm{min}}55.5^{\mathrm s};$$
$$\delta_{\text{Mizar}}=\delta_1=54^\circ55'31'';\qquad\alpha_{\text{Sirius}}=\alpha_2=6^{\mathrm h}45^{\mathrm{min}};$$
$$\delta_{\text{Sirius}}=\delta_2=-16^\circ43'.$$

[[figure p3-fig1]]

Note

$$\ln(1-x)\approx-x\quad\text{for }x\ll1;\qquad e^x\approx1+x\quad\text{for }x\ll1.$$

solution.incompleteReason: The available preliminary Problem 3B key uses seven Big Dipper stars, whereas the final photographed problem asks about four Mizar-system stars and uncertainties. No matching final key for c, d, f, g or the error estimates was found. The compatible Sun calculation and explicitly conditional earlier Sirius calculation are reproduced; the earlier angular calculation is identified as a source discrepancy.
solution.statement: This is a partial recovery from the preliminary Problem 3B solution, not a complete official solution to the final Mizar version. The changed stellar table is not interchangeable with the final one.

sections.title: a) Sun — compatible calculation
sections.statement:
$$\log\frac{E_{\text{Sun,Earth}}}{E_{\text{Sun,Planet}}}=-0.4(m_{\text{Sun,Earth}}-m_{\text{Sun,Planet}});$$
$$E_{\text{Sun,Earth}}=\frac{L_{\text{Sun}}}{4\pi d_{\text{Sun,Earth}}^2};\qquad E_{\text{Sun,Planet}}=\frac{L_{\text{Sun}}}{4\pi d_{\text{Sun,Planet}}^2}.$$

The key uses $d_{\text{Sun,Earth}}=1\,\mathrm{AU}$, $d_{\text{Sun,Planet}}=2.6\,\mathrm{pc}=2.6\cdot206265\,\mathrm{AU}$ and $m_{\text{Sun,Earth}}=-26.78^{\mathrm m}$, and obtains

$$m_{\text{Sun,Planet}}=1.87^{\mathrm m}.$$

sections.title: b) Earlier Sirius calculation — different supplied data
sections.statement:
The preliminary key assumes $L_{\text{Sirius}}=25L_{\text{Sun}}$, which is not supplied in the final problem. With $d_{\text{Sirius,Planet}}=10\,\mathrm{AU}$, it writes

$$\log\frac{E_{\text{Sirius,Planet}}}{E_{\text{Sun,Planet}}}=-0.4(m_{\text{Sirius,Planet}}-m_{\text{Sun,Planet}}),$$

and obtains $m_{\text{Sirius,Planet}}=-25.255^{\mathrm m}$ using $m_{\text{Sun,Planet}}=1.87^{\mathrm m}$.

This is the earlier key's result under its extra luminosity assumption. The final question instead supplies the apparent Sirius magnitude measured from Earth; the value above is not presented as a verified answer for that changed data.

sections.title: e) Earlier angular calculation — printed discrepancy
sections.statement:
The earlier key uses the same printed coordinate pair, but calls the first star Big Dipper rather than Mizar. It applies

$$\cos a=\cos b\cos c+\sin b\sin c\cos A,\qquad A=90^\circ,$$

then sets $a=\Delta\theta$, $b=\Delta\alpha$, $c=\Delta\delta$ and writes

$$\cos\Delta\theta=\cos\Delta\alpha\cos\Delta\delta;$$
$$\Delta\alpha=6^{\mathrm h}38^{\mathrm{min}}55.5^{\mathrm s}\approx100^\circ;$$
$$\Delta\delta=71^\circ38'31''\approx72.4^\circ;$$
$$\cos\Delta\theta=\cos100^\circ\cos72.4^\circ=(-0.173648177)(0.30236989)=-0.05250598;$$
$$\Delta\theta\approx90.3^\circ\approx90^\circ.$$

**Source note:** these are the printed earlier calculation and approximations, which are inconsistent. They are retained as a comparison with the archived key, not as a corrected or validated solution of the final question. Its seven-star luminosity, distance and magnitude calculations do not answer the final four-star Mizar problem and have not been imported here.
